extracted.intended_audience: educational institutions, Title IX coordinators, and compliance/legal staff responsible for implementing Title IX
extracted.subtask_description: Clarification of recipients' obligations under §106.40 regarding reasonable modifications, voluntary leave, and comparable programs for students who are pregnant or experiencing pregnancy-related conditions, and the Title IX Coordinator's coordinating role. Guidance explains interactions with other federal laws, privacy, delegation, and related procedural points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individualized reasonable modifications requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must make reasonable modifications to its policies, practices, or procedures as necessary to prevent sex discrimination and ensure equal access to the recipient's education program or activity for a student who is pregnant or experiencing pregnancy-related conditions (§106.40(b)(3)(ii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modifications must be considered on an individualized basis to each student's pregnancy or related condition and needs; recipients may consider factors such as a student's preferred modification, alternative modifications, and feasibility. A recipient has discretion among multiple reasonable modifications but bears the burden of demonstrating that a proposed modification would fundamentally alter the nature of the education program. Examples include breaks for lactation or health needs, online or homebound instruction, extra time to complete coursework for travel to receive care, or temporary adjustments (e.g., larger desk, elevator access).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient implements; Title IX Coordinator coordinates and retains oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: The recipient, not the Title IX Coordinator, is ultimately responsible for implementing requests for reasonable modifications and other specific actions under §106.40(b)(3)(ii)-(vi). The Title IX Coordinator's role is to coordinate those actions and retain ultimate oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulatory text was revised to clarify that the Title IX Coordinator may delegate duties but must maintain oversight to ensure consistent compliance. The Title IX Coordinator can serve as a central point of contact, communicate approved modifications, and ensure staff perform their roles; however, delegation is permitted to fit institutional structures and avoid overburdening the Coordinator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation of duties permitted with oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient may delegate specific duties related to providing reasonable modifications because of pregnancy or related conditions to other personnel or departments, including those who support students with disabilities, as long as the Title IX Coordinator retains ultimate oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegation enables assignment to personnel best positioned to perform duties, addresses conflicts of interest, and aligns with administrative structures. Recipients may delegate provision of reasonable modifications to other employees or departments, provided processes are consistent with §106.40(b)(3)(ii) and the Coordinator ensures compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: No regulatory requirement to document reasonable modifications (Coordinator)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations removed the proposed requirement that the Title IX Coordinator must 'document' reasonable modifications; recipients are not required by §106.40(b)(3)(ii) to maintain documentation of compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may choose to voluntarily maintain records, but such records would be subject to §106.44(j) restrictions on disclosure of personally identifiable information. The removal aimed to decrease administrative burden and address privacy concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation with disability services/IEP/Section 504 teams is fact-specific, not mandatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are not required to consult with disability support staff, a student's IEP team, or Section 504 team in every case when providing reasonable modifications because of pregnancy or related conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether consultation is required depends on facts—e.g., if a pregnancy-related request affects placement or educational delivery (such as a medically-necessary six-week leave), IEP/504 teams likely must convene. Conversely, for requests unrelated to the disability (e.g., lactation breaks for a student with a vision disability), requiring such consultation may be unnecessary or violate privacy. Recipients should weigh privacy, relevance, and educational impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary leave of absence requirement for medically necessary time
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §106.40(b)(3)(iv), a recipient must allow a student who is pregnant or experiencing pregnancy-related conditions to voluntarily take a leave of absence covering at minimum the time deemed medically necessary by the student's licensed healthcare provider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave covers pregnancy, childbirth, termination of pregnancy, lactation, related medical conditions, and recovery. Leave is distinct from reasonable modifications and is intended to ensure continued access to education during medically necessary absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable modifications and leave apply to termination of pregnancy and related care
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient's obligation to provide reasonable modifications or a voluntary leave of absence includes complications arising from termination of pregnancy and out-of-State travel for pregnancy-related healthcare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such modifications (e.g., online instruction during recovery, extra time to complete coursework when travel is necessary) are considered non-discriminatory access measures and do not constitute providing or paying for abortion services. Recipients have no educational need to determine illegality or specifics of an abortion; requests for invasive/irrelevant information should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 1688 (abortion neutrality) does not bar modifications or leaves
rubrics_metrics.description: 20 U.S.C. 1688, which states Title IX cannot 'require or prohibit' providing or paying for abortion-related benefits/services, does not prohibit reasonable modifications or voluntary leaves related to termination of pregnancy under Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department interprets section 1688 as limited to performance/payment for abortion; modifications and leaves are access measures, not benefits/services to perform or pay for abortion. Also, 1688's second sentence forbids penalties for seeking abortion, so recipients should avoid policies that penalize students for seeking or receiving abortion care. Requiring different or invasive information for abortion-related modifications could contravene Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary or invasive information requests about pregnancy/abortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients should not ask students for sensitive or specific healthcare information about the origin, timeline, or manner of pregnancy-related care (including abortion) as a condition of providing reasonable modifications or leave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treating abortion-related requests differently than other temporary medical conditions may violate Title IX. Invasive inquiries (e.g., how pregnancy occurred) can reflect sex stereotypes or chill students from seeking modifications; information gathering should be limited to what is education-related and necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX obligations distinct from ADA/Section 504 obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: A pregnancy-related condition need not qualify as a disability under the ADA or Section 504 for the student to be eligible for reasonable modifications under Title IX; obligations under §106.40(b)(3)(ii) are separate from disability law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reasonable modifications framework draws from Title II of the ADA and invites collaboration to identify individualized required modifications, but it does not transform pregnancy into a disability under ADA. Recipients must still comply with all applicable civil rights laws (ADA, Section 504, Title VII/PDA, PWFA), and coordination across laws may be necessary in particular cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation applies regardless of student also being an employee (student-employee)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §106.40(b)(3)(ii), recipients must provide reasonable modifications to an individual defined as a 'student' (person who has gained admission) even if that person is also an employee of the recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recipient must offer and make reasonable modifications sufficient to allow the employee-student to continue educational progress; grievance procedures in §106.45 (and if applicable §106.46) apply to complaints alleging failure to take actions under §106.40(b)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations do not extend reasonable modifications to applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declined to require recipients to apply §106.40(b)(3)(ii) to applicants for admission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests that applicants be covered were considered but the Department retained the existing scope; see discussion of §106.21(c)(1) for more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and meaning of the term 'reasonable modifications'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department retained the term 'reasonable modifications' rather than 'reasonable accommodations' because it fits the regulatory framework and aligns with Title II of the ADA (28 CFR 35.130(b)(7)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the final regulations, a reasonable modification can be implemented for just one student or as a broader policy/procedural change affecting many (e.g., extending a deadline for all students). 'Modification' was judged less confusing and more appropriate than other terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-benefit and scope limitations: not extended beyond students
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department concluded that costs/burdens of implementing §106.40(b)(3)(ii) are modest and decline to extend reasonable modifications beyond students who are pregnant or experiencing pregnancy-related conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing obligations (e.g., temporary medical condition accommodations) mean many modifications are minor. While recipients may offer leave/modifications to parents or caregivers, any such rules must not treat students differently on the basis of sex (e.g., granting bonding leave only to one sex would violate Title IX). The Department views the rule as effective to prevent sex discrimination and facilitate educational access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary separate programs must be truly voluntary and comparable
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation in any separate portion of a recipient's education program or activity based on pregnancy or related conditions must be voluntary and such programs must be comparable to those offered to students who are not pregnant or parenting (§106.40(b)(1) and (3)(iii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must not coerce, pressure, or force pregnant students into separate or inferior programs. The Department declined to adopt a 'substantially equal' standard or to further define 'comparable' beyond existing regulatory text; 'voluntarily' has long been interpreted to prohibit coercion. OCR guidance has reiterated this longstanding policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable modifications are remedial measures to prevent sex discrimination, not preferential treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing reasonable modifications based on pregnancy or related conditions is intended to prevent sex discrimination and ensure equal access, not to provide preferential treatment based on sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title IX regulations have historically required proactive measures for pregnant students; denying reasonable modifications uniquely deprives a student of educational opportunity because of sex. The Department rejects arguments that these requirements improperly expand disability law or conflict with Title VII; education-context rules can and have included protections unique to students.
